lesson.title: Rounding and bounded random choices
lesson.summary: Implement chooseIndex(sample, size). Accept a finite Number sample from 0 inclusive to 1 exclusive, and an integer size 1..1000. Return a clamped index 0..size-1 or null for invalid inputs. Do not call Math.random inside this function.

Number.isInteger(size) returns true only when size is an integer Number, without converting strings. Reject invalid inputs with null; use supplied samples to test boundaries rather than demand a particular random outcome.

lesson.title: Number precision and safe integers
lesson.summary: Implement safeAdd(a, b). Return their sum only when both inputs and the result satisfy Number.isSafeInteger; otherwise return null.
explanation: Number uses binary floating-point. Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 9007199254740991: within the safe integer range, distinct neighboring integers are represented distinctly. Some larger integers are representable, but not every neighbor is.

Number.isSafeInteger(value) returns true for an integer Number within the safe range, and false for fractions, strings or unsafe magnitudes. safeAdd accepts two values and returns null unless both inputs and their sum are safe integers. A safe pair can still produce an unsafe sum.

The unsafe expressions Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 and Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2 produce the same Number. Seeing no decimal point does not prove exact integer arithmetic. For larger exact counters use the separate BigInt lesson, not guessed rounding.

lesson.title: BigInt arithmetic
lesson.summary: Implement addCounters(left, right) for valid decimal integer strings. Convert each directly with BigInt, return a BigInt sum, and do not pass through Number.
explanation: BigInt represents integers without the Number safe-range restriction. A literal such as 2n is a BigInt, not a Number. BigInt(text) converts a valid integer string directly, avoiding a rounded Number intermediate. BigInt does not represent fractions.

Adding a BigInt to a Number throws TypeError; write 1n rather than 1 when adding to a BigInt. String(bigintValue) produces decimal text without the literal suffix n. lesson.title: Short-circuit AND value flow
lesson.summary: Implement readWhen(flag, reader). Return flag && reader() exactly, preserving falsy flag values and the reader result. Do not call reader when flag is falsy.
explanation: The && operator is not a Boolean-conversion function. It evaluates its left operand first. If that value is falsy, it returns that value without evaluating the right side. Otherwise it evaluates and returns the right side.

readWhen(flag, reader) returns flag && reader(). reader is a supplied zero-argument function. If flag is 0, the result is the number 0 and reader is never called. If flag is true, the result is whatever reader returns, even an empty string. The example () => "ready" is a zero-argument arrow function that returns "ready" when called; passing it does not call it yet.

Use this behavior when preserving the actual operand result is intended. If an API requires a Boolean result instead, explicitly convert it rather than assuming && always returns true or false. This extends the earlier ||/?? lesson without changing their rules.

lesson.title: Switch and fall-through
lesson.summary: Implement delivery(kind) with grouped letter/card cases returning "small", parcel returning "large", and all other inputs returning "unknown". Match exact strings.
explanation: switch(value) compares its value against case expressions using strict equality. A matching case starts execution there. It does not automatically stop at the next case label; without break or return, execution can fall through.

delivery(kind) groups "letter" and "card" before one return. A parcel gets a different result, and default handles anything else. return exits the whole function, so these branches do not need an additional break.

Grouping adjacent labels deliberately shares one action. If you only assign a result and then continue into another case, add break when that continuation is not intended. A string "1" does not match numeric case 1.

lesson.title: Break continue and do-while
lesson.summary: Implement positiveBeforeStop(values): scan integers in order, skip negatives, stop at the first zero, and return the preceding positive values in a new array. Keep the supplied oneVisit demonstration unchanged.
explanation: continue skips the remaining body of the current loop iteration, then proceeds with the loop’s next iteration. In positiveBeforeStop, negative values are skipped rather than copied. This does not stop the entire loop.
break exits the nearest loop immediately. Here the sentinel 0 ends collection, so positive values after that point are not visited or returned. These two control actions solve different problems.

A do...while loop runs its body before testing its condition, so it runs at least once. In oneVisit(limit), count is incremented before count < limit is checked. Thus even limit 0 produces one visit. This is a separate demonstration, not a reason to force do...while into the collection task. JSON.stringify(value) formats these simple arrays/objects as JSON text for display; it returns a string and does not edit the value.

lesson.title: Default and rest parameters
lesson.summary: Implement labelList(prefix = "Items", ...items) returning prefix + ": " + the comma-joined items. Apply the default only for omitted/undefined prefix and preserve an empty prefix.
explanation: A default parameter is used when the caller omits that argument or supplies undefined. It is not used for null, zero or an empty string. This distinction preserves intentionally supplied values.

The final parameter ...items gathers remaining arguments into a new array. Rest must be last. In labelList(prefix = "Items", ...items), the first argument belongs to prefix and all later arguments become items.

items.join(",") returns a string containing the items separated by commas, without changing the array. Template interpolation turns the supplied prefix into text. This lesson accepts printable simple values; it does not validate a user-facing schema.

lesson.title: Arithmetic operators and precedence
lesson.summary: Implement priceTotal(base, count, fee) as base * count + fee. Keep the fee outside the repeated item cost. Use the visible examples to explain division, remainder and exponentiation separately.
explanation: In 2 + 3 * 4, multiplication runs before addition, giving 14. Parentheses change the grouping: (2 + 3) * 4 gives 20. ** means exponentiation, so 2 ** 3 is 8; it is not the same as multiplying by three.

With Number operands, 7 / 2 is 3.5 rather than integer division. The % operator gives a remainder; a negative dividend can produce a negative remainder, such as -7 % 3 being -1. Do not assume it is a nonnegative mathematical modulo.

priceTotal(base, count, fee) multiplies base by count before adding one fee. Inputs are ordinary finite Numbers within the small lesson range. A different grouping would multiply the fee too, changing the meaning rather than just the style.

lesson.title: String search, slicing and transformation
lesson.summary: Implement preview(text, limit) for ASCII strings and a nonnegative integer limit. Return a lower-case prefix without changing the original text.
explanation: text.includes(part) returns a Boolean telling whether a substring occurs. text.indexOf(part) returns its first zero-based UTF-16 index, or -1 if missing. Zero is a valid found position, so do not test indexOf directly as a truthy/falsy found flag.

text.slice(start, end) returns text from start up to but excluding end; it does not change the original. toLowerCase() and toUpperCase() return case-converted strings. These operations are not a complete locale-aware or Unicode-normalization policy.

text.replace("cat", "dog") returns text with the first matching literal occurrence replaced. This call does not replace every occurrence. Strings are immutable: assign the result if you want a name to refer to the changed text.

preview(text, limit) returns the first limit UTF-16 code units, converted to lower case. Inputs here are ASCII text and a nonnegative integer limit, so the exercise does not accidentally split a surrogate pair. Unicode boundaries are handled separately in lesson45.

lesson.title: String search, slicing and transformation
lesson.summary: Implement preview(text, limit) for ASCII strings and a nonnegative integer limit. Return a lower-case prefix without changing the original text.
explanation: text.includes(part) returns a Boolean telling whether a substring occurs. text.indexOf(part) returns its first zero-based UTF-16 index, or -1 if missing. Zero is a valid found position, so do not test indexOf directly as a truthy/falsy found flag.

text.slice(start, end) returns text from start up to but excluding end; it does not change the original. toLowerCase() and toUpperCase() return case-converted strings. These operations are not a complete locale-aware or Unicode-normalization policy.

text.replace("cat", "dog") returns text with the first matching literal occurrence replaced. This call does not replace every occurrence. Strings are immutable: assign the result if you want a name to refer to the changed text.

preview(text, limit) returns the first limit UTF-16 code units, converted to lower case. Inputs here are ASCII text and a nonnegative integer limit, so the exercise does not accidentally split a surrogate pair. Unicode boundaries are handled separately in lesson45.

lesson.title: Array search and controlled editing
lesson.summary: Implement replaceFirst for string arrays. Preserve the original, replace only the first exact match, and return a distinct copy even if no match exists.
explanation: Array.indexOf(value) returns the first matching index or -1. For the string arrays in this lesson it finds exact matching text. A missing value must be handled before splice: using index -1 would target the last element rather than do nothing.

array.splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) removes deleteCount elements at start and inserts any supplied items there. It mutates that array and returns a new array of the removed elements. To preserve a caller’s source, first make a shallow copy with slice().

forEach(callback) calls the callback for each present element and returns undefined. A callback’s returned values are ignored; use map when you want a result array. The example uses forEach to accumulate a total only as a clear side-effect demonstration.

replaceFirst(values, oldValue, newValue) copies the input string array, finds its first exact oldValue, replaces that one entry if found, and returns the copy. Leave later duplicates unchanged and never remove the final entry on a miss. JSON.stringify(value) formats these simple arrays/objects as JSON text for display; it returns a string and does not edit the value.
Implement replaceFirst for string arrays. Preserve the original, replace only the first exact match, and return a distinct copy even if no match exists.

lesson.title: Rounding and bounded random choices
lesson.summary: Implement chooseIndex(sample, size). Accept a finite Number sample from 0 inclusive to 1 exclusive, and an integer size 1..1000. Return a clamped index 0..size-1 or null for invalid inputs. Do not call Math.random inside this function.
explanation: Math.floor(value) returns the greatest integer not above value; Math.ceil(value) returns the least integer not below it. For -1.2, floor is -2 and ceil is -1. These are direction rules, not simply removing the fractional digits.

Math.random() returns a Number at least zero and less than one. It is not a cryptographic security tool. Multiplying a sample by a positive item count and taking floor normally maps it to an index; floating-point rounding near boundaries should be considered when generalizing arbitrary ranges.

chooseIndex(sample, size) accepts a sample in [0,1) and a positive integer size from 1 through 1000. It returns Math.min(size - 1, Math.floor(sample * size)), explicitly clamping the upper index against rounding. Math.min selects the smaller numeric argument. Number.isInteger(size) returns true only when size is an integer Number, without converting strings. Reject invalid inputs with null; use supplied samples to test boundaries rather than demand a particular random outcome.

Implement chooseIndex(sample, size). Accept a finite Number sample from 0 inclusive to 1 exclusive, and an integer size 1..1000. Return a clamped index 0..size-1 or null for invalid inputs. Do not call Math.random inside this function.
